tips.title: Concede first, then take the point
tips.text: Nothing disarms a stubborn official like agreement: "Dass das Geld kostet, steht außer Frage. Gleichwohl …" — you give a centimetre and take the argument.

tips.title: A fronting that persuades
tips.text: "Gerade JETZT müssen wir handeln" or "Verschieben können wir das Projekt immer noch" — put the pressure word first and the mayor hears it twice.

speaking.topic: You are a stubborn, budget-obsessed mayor; I lobby you to fund a project of my choosing. Object realistically and yield only to well-built arguments. I must use at least three Funktionsverbgefüge and one deliberate emphasis fronting — track them and name them in the feedback.
practisePoints: Concession-then-rebuttal argument structure
Funktionsverbgefüge deployed naturally under pressure
One planted Vorfeld fronting for emphasis
scoringCriteria: three correct FVG woven in, not bolted on
the fronting lands and reads as intentional
priorityErrors: FVG with wrong preposition or article

help.intro: The hardest part of formal writing is restraint. You write the long version, then the ruthless short one — and the AI grades whether each function-verb phrase earned its seat.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Density is a dial, not a goal
tips.text: Three FVG in 150 words read as command; eight read as a ministry memo parody. If two FVG land in one sentence, demote one to its simple verb.

tips.title: Summarise demands, not sentences
tips.text: For the 40-word version, do not shorten your sentences — list your stance and your demand, then write two new sentences that carry only those.

speaking.topic: A 150-word position paper plus its 40-word executive summary, graded above all on Funktionsverbgefüge density without stiffness.
practisePoints: FVG density that elevates rather than inflates
Compression: 150 words to 40 without losing the demand
A structurally marked concession
scoringCriteria: FVG used well and judged honestly
summary fidelity within the word limit
priorityErrors: FVG stacked until the prose goes stiff
speaking.material:
Writing task:
- Pick one workplace or civic issue (I may propose one if you prefer). Write a position paper of about 150 words: clear stance, one concession, one counter-argument, one concrete demand.
- Then compress it into a 40-word executive summary that a busy reader could act on — no new content, no lost demand.
Rubric (grade against this):
- 3–5 Funktionsverbgefüge, each earning its place (biggest weight): flag any that stiffen the prose as errors.
- Collocations exact (Kritik üben an, Maßnahmen ergreifen …).
- Concession structurally marked (zugegeben / zwar … doch).
- The summary keeps stance AND demand within 40 words.
- Register: consistently formal, no colloquial bleed.

help.intro: Same pool, same burst pipe, two newspapers that could not sound less alike. You write the front page twice, and the AI hunts for the one word that betrays the wrong paper.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: The same fact, two voices
tips.text: Tabloid: "Bad dicht — und der Bürgermeister wusste es!" Broadsheet: "Der Bürgermeister räumte ein, seit dem Frühjahr von den Schäden Kenntnis gehabt zu haben."

tips.title: Sentence length is register
tips.text: Before word choice, check rhythm: tabloid sentences average six words, broadsheet ones twenty. Get the rhythm right and half the register work is done.

speaking.topic: One story, two publications: I narrate the same event first as a tabloid would, then as a broadsheet. Grade register purity per version, sentence by sentence.
practisePoints: Tabloid register: punch, outrage, colloquial verbs
Broadsheet register: FVG, attribution, measured syntax
Keeping the facts identical across both tellings
priorityErrors: broadsheet words leaking into the tabloid or vice versa
speaking.material:
Story skeleton:
- The event: a small-town swimming pool closes for the summer because of a burst pipe; the mayor knew about the damage since spring; families are furious; repairs start in August.
- Beat 1, tabloid (BILD voice): short punchy sentences, outrage, exclamation, colloquial verbs (kriegen, dichtmachen), a furious quote from "Mutter Sabine (34)".
- Beat 2, broadsheet (FAZ voice): measured periods, FVG and exact collocations (Kritik üben an, Maßnahmen ergreifen), an attributed official statement, no exclamation marks.
- Same facts in both — invent nothing new for version two.
- After both, name one sentence from each version that would be impossible in the other, and say why.

help.intro: The daily C2 task nobody teaches: hearing management prose and saying what it means. You catch a formal statement by ear and hand it on in human German — nothing lost, nothing stiff.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Translate the FVG down
tips.text: "zum Abschluss bringen" becomes "beenden", "zur Verfügung stellen" becomes "die Leute gehen zu …". If a chunk from the statement survives verbatim, you have not retold it.

tips.title: Relaxed has a floor
tips.text: Coffee-machine German is casual, not careless: "Atlas wird dichtgemacht, voll übel" undershoots. Aim for "Atlas läuft Ende des Jahres aus" — easy, but still office-worthy.

speaking.topic: You read me a formal written statement aloud; I render it for a colleague in relaxed but still professional spoken German — same content, one register down.
practisePoints: Decoding FVG-heavy formal prose by ear
Down-shifting register without losing precision
Keeping all facts through the shift
priorityErrors: FVG copied into the spoken version
speaking.material:
The piece (read it to me aloud, twice if I ask):
"Sehr geehrte Mitarbeiterinnen und Mitarbeiter, die Geschäftsleitung hat nach eingehender Prüfung die Entscheidung getroffen, das Projekt Atlas zum Jahresende zum Abschluss zu bringen. Die frei werdenden Kapazitäten werden ab Januar dem Bereich Kundenservice zur Verfügung gestellt. Wir sind uns bewusst, dass dieser Schritt mit Unannehmlichkeiten verbunden ist, und nehmen diese nicht leichtfertig in Kauf. Etwaige Rückfragen richten Sie bitte an die Personalabteilung."
My task afterwards:
- Retell it to a colleague at the coffee machine: relaxed, spoken, professional — no FVG, but no slang collapse either.
- All four facts must survive: Atlas ends in December, people move to Kundenservice in January, management admits it is inconvenient, questions go to HR.
- Then ask me two checking questions about details I glossed.

help.intro: The stress test before the exam: journalists who twist your words in real time. Your job is not to win the room — it is to stay precise, stay formal, and correct the record every time.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: The correction formula
tips.text: "Das habe ich so nicht gesagt. Gesagt habe ich, dass …" — note the fronting: putting "Gesagt" first turns your correction into emphasis. M11 grammar, live under fire.

tips.title: Bridge, don't bite
tips.text: A loaded question wants a defensive answer. Concede one word, then pivot: "Unbequem ist die Entscheidung, ja — entscheidend aber ist …" and you are back on message.

speaking.topic: A press conference. I am the spokesperson defending an unpopular decision my organisation has made; you play several journalists who interrupt, bait me with loaded questions, and misquote what I just said. Stay hostile but realistic.
practisePoints: Correcting a misquote calmly and precisely
Bridging from a loaded question back to the message
Formal register held under interruption
targetVocabulary: Das habe ich so nicht gesagt.

help.intro: The M11 gate: an interview where the AI yanks the register lever mid-sentence. Same content, new voice, no pause. Pass it and the final module unlocks — your best score counts.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Finish the thought, not the sentence
tips.text: On "formell!" you may abandon the sentence, never the thought: restart the clause in the new register and carry the content over. Content continuity is scored separately.

tips.title: Three gears, three verbs
tips.text: Keep the triplet as your gearbox: kriegen — bekommen — erhalten. Whichever gear is called, shift the verb first and the rest of the register engages behind it.

speaking.topic: The style-command exam. Interview me on everyday and professional topics, but hold the content constant and switch the register on your command MID-ANSWER: call "formell!", "neutral!" or "salopp!" and I must re-voice the running answer instantly. Do this at least four times across the interview.
practisePoints: Instant register switches without losing the thread
FVG and exact collocations on demand in formal mode
Colloquial mode that is loose but controlled
Emphasis fronting used at least once, deliberately
priorityErrors: FVG with broken preposition or article

help.intro: The words no dictionary can hand you: jein, Feierabend, the many lives of doch. Your AI serves them in tiny dialogues and grades whether you feel what they do, not what they "mean".

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: doch has two day jobs
tips.text: Unstressed inside a sentence, doch nudges ("Komm doch mit!"). Stressed and alone, it overturns a negative: "Magst du keinen Kaffee?" — "Doch!" means yes, I do.

tips.title: Feierabend is a place
tips.text: Think of Feierabend as somewhere you GO, not a time: "nach Feierabend", "schönen Feierabend!" — the workday ends and a small private festival begins. No English word attends.

speaking.topic: Untranslatables and colloquialisms, served inside mini-dialogues: I translate the EFFECT of the marked word (not the word), then answer the dialogue line in matching register.
practisePoints: Explaining the pragmatic effect, not a dictionary gloss
doch in both jobs: pressure particle and yes-I-do
Replying inside the dialogue's colloquial register
priorityErrors: translating the word instead of its effect
speaking.material:
Serve each mini-dialogue, mark the target word, ask me for its effect, then for my in-register reply:
1. "Kommst du mit?" — "*Jein* … kommt drauf an, wer noch da ist." (jein = yes-and-no, hedged)
2. "Endlich *Feierabend*!" (Feierabend = the sacred end of the working day, almost a small holiday)
3. "Du kommst *doch* mit, oder?" (doch = hopeful pressure: contradiction pre-empted)
4. "Magst du keinen Kaffee?" — "*Doch*!" (doch = yes-I-do, overturning a negative)
5. "Guck *mal* her." (mal = softener, makes the imperative light)
6. "*Haste* mal 'nen Stift?" (haste = hast du, rapid colloquial)
7. "Das ist *halt* so." (halt = resigned that's-just-how-it-is)
8. "Na, *isses* weit noch?" (isses = ist es, spoken contraction)
9. "Der Film war ganz gut — aber *eben* kein Meisterwerk." (eben = precisely-that, confirming a limit)
10. "*Na ja*, war schon okay." (na ja = lukewarm concession)
For each: half the points for naming the effect precisely, half for a reply whose register matches the dialogue.

help.intro: No material, no preparation, no mercy: three topics you did not pick, cut mid-sentence. The score rewards how gracefully you wobble — repair is the skill, not perfection.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Name the cut
tips.text: When the topic jumps, say so: "Wie dem auch sei — zum neuen Thema …" Naming the swerve out loud IS discourse management, and it buys your brain the second it needs.

tips.title: Repair beats silence
tips.text: A native speaker lost for words says "wie soll ich sagen …" and keeps the floor. Two seconds of silence costs more than any grammar slip in this exercise.

speaking.topic: Free conversation without a safety net: pick three random topics of escalating abstraction (an object, a social question, a philosophical one) and change topic MID-SENTENCE at least twice. Weight the grading towards flexibility and repair strategies, not polish.
practisePoints: Following an abrupt topic cut without stalling
Repair phrases: wo waren wir, wie soll ich sagen, Moment
Holding depth even on a topic I did not choose
priorityErrors: retreating to B-level simplicity when surprised

help.intro: Defend the sock conspiracy like your career depends on it. The joke is the frame; the graded content is pure argumentation under cross-examination — dodging costs more than losing.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Concede the fact, keep the thesis
tips.text: "Zugegeben, niemand hat je eine Socke emigrieren sehen — doch gerade DAS beweist, wie gut sie es planen." Concession plus reframe answers any question without surrender.

tips.title: A joke is not an answer
tips.text: The frame is absurd; your moves must not be. If the AI asks "Wohin emigrieren sie denn?", name a destination and argue for it. Laughing the question off is scored as a dodge.

speaking.topic: The Absurde These game: I draw an absurd thesis and defend it against your genuine cross-examination. Argue back hard — treat my thesis as if it mattered.
practisePoints: Building arguments for a position I do not hold
Answering hostile questions instead of dodging
Rhetorical tools (fronting, particles) under fire
priorityErrors: humour used as a substitute for argument
speaking.material:
Game rules:
- Offer me three absurd theses to draw from, e.g.: "Socken verschwinden nicht — sie emigrieren", "Montage sollten verboten werden", "Pflanzen hören uns zu und sind enttäuscht".
- I defend my drawn thesis for 5 exchanges against real cross-examination: demand evidence, expose contradictions, offer tempting outs.
- Scoring per exchange: full points for a substantive defence (concession + counter, analogy, reframing).
- Conceding a round costs points; DODGING a question costs more — an answered absurdity beats an evaded one.
- Bonus points for one rhetorical fronting and one correctly placed particle (doch, eben, ja) per exchange.
- After 5 exchanges, convert my points to the final score.

help.intro: The listening skill C2 actually demands: real people mumble, contract and drop syllables. You hear the polished and the street version of one scene and prove you can map between them.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Contractions are receptive vocabulary
tips.text: You need to UNDERSTAND isses, haste and 'nen instantly — you rarely need to say them. Decode them like vocabulary: each one expands to exactly one standard form.

tips.title: haste smuggles in du
tips.text: haste is not just fast speech — it is "hast du". The colloquial stranger switched to du without asking. Hearing that social move inside a contraction is the C2 catch.

speaking.topic: You speak the same short scene twice — once in neutral standard German, once colloquial and lightly dialect-tinged — and I map one version onto the other.
practisePoints: Decoding contractions at speed (isses, haste, 'nen)
Mapping colloquial onto standard forms precisely
Hearing when a contraction changes politeness, not just sound
priorityErrors: missing the politeness shift in haste
speaking.material:
The piece (perform BOTH versions aloud, colloquial one noticeably faster):
Version 1, neutral: "Guten Abend. Ist es noch weit bis zum Bahnhof? Ich habe meinen Zug verpasst und weiß nicht, ob heute noch einer fährt. Haben Sie vielleicht einen Fahrplan? Das wäre wirklich nett von Ihnen."
Version 2, colloquial: "'n Abend! Isses noch weit bis zum Bahnhof? Hab meinen Zug verpasst und keine Ahnung, ob heut überhaupt noch einer fährt. Haste vielleicht 'nen Fahrplan? Wär echt nett."
My tasks afterwards:
- Retell the scene's content once, register-neutral.
- Map five pairs across the versions (isses ↔ ist es, haste ↔ haben Sie, 'nen ↔ einen, heut ↔ heute, wär ↔ das wäre) and say what each contraction does.
- Note the one pair that also shifts POLITENESS, not just sound (haste = du-form vs. Haben Sie = Sie-form).
- Then quiz me: speak two NEW colloquial lines in the same style and have me render them in neutral standard German.

help.intro: One bike lane, two truths. The satirist and the reporter agree on more than they seem to — your job is to find exactly where, and to write the one summary both could sign.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Satire exaggerates around a true bone
tips.text: Strip each satirical sentence to its checkable core: the Blaskapelle may be invented, the unguarded crossing is not. Mediation starts by sorting bone from flesh.

tips.title: "wird geprüft" is a verdict
tips.text: Administrative passive ("wird geprüft", "liegt noch nicht vor") reports inaction in the costume of action. Reading that costume is C2 comprehension of the sober text too.

speaking.topic: Two texts about the same event — a satirical column and a sober report. The questions force me to mediate between their claims rather than summarise either.
practisePoints: Extracting the shared factual core of opposed texts
Naming how satire transforms a fact
Writing one mediated summary fair to both
scoringCriteria: satirical mechanics explained, not just felt
the mediated summary balances both texts
priorityErrors: adopting one text's framing as fact
summary that averages instead of mediates
speaking.material:
Text A, satirical column (show it exactly like this):
"Es ist vollbracht: Unsere Stadt hat eine Fahrradstraße. Ganze dreihundert Meter, festlich eröffnet mit Blaskapelle, endend — man ahnt es — an einer vierspurigen Kreuzung ohne Ampel. Der Bürgermeister sprach von einem Meilenstein. Ein Meilenstein ist bekanntlich ein Stein, an dem man vorbeifährt. Die Radfahrer der Stadt danken es ihm, sofern sie die Kreuzung überleben."

Text B, sober report:
"Am Samstag wurde die erste Fahrradstraße der Stadt eröffnet. Der 300 Meter lange Abschnitt in der Gartenstraße ist Teil eines Konzepts, das bis 2030 insgesamt zwölf Kilometer umfassen soll. Die Anbindung an die Kreuzung Nordring wird laut Stadtverwaltung in einem zweiten Bauabschnitt geprüft; ein Zeitplan hierfür liegt noch nicht vor. Der ADFC begrüßte den Schritt, mahnte jedoch ein höheres Tempo an."

Ask me (one at a time, in German):
1. Welchen Sachverhalt bestätigen BEIDE Texte übereinstimmend?
2. Die Kreuzung: Was macht die Satire daraus, was der Bericht — und widersprechen sich die beiden wirklich?
3. Wie funktioniert die Meilenstein-Pointe sprachlich?
4. Der Bericht schreibt "wird geprüft" und "liegt noch nicht vor" — was leistet diese Behördensprache, und wie übersetzt die Satire sie?
5. Formulieren Sie EINE faire Zusammenfassung des Ereignisses, die beiden Texten gerecht wird — je ein Element aus beiden.
6. Wo hört die Satire auf zu übertreiben und sagt schlicht die Wahrheit?

help.intro: Two furious flatmates, one of you. You must speak Jonas's language AND Frau Petrova's, find what each actually needs, and leave the room with a written deal both say yes to.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Mirror before you mediate
tips.text: Restate each grievance in its owner's register: to Jonas "Dich nervt, dass du ständig der Böse bist", to Frau Petrova "Sie wünschen sich verbindliche Absprachen." Only a heard party negotiates.

tips.title: The Konjunktiv of peace
tips.text: "Der Kompromiss läge darin, dass …" — the Konjunktiv II offers without imposing. A mediator who says "ihr müsst" has already lost the room.

speaking.topic: Mediation: you play BOTH flatmates in clearly different voices — Jonas (colloquial, hurt, interrupts) and Frau Petrova (formal, icy, precise) — at war over noise, cleaning and a broken lamp. I broker a compromise and, at the end, dictate it as a short written agreement both explicitly accept. Do not let either accept it until it addresses their core grievance.
practisePoints: Mirroring each party in their own register
Mediation language: beide Seiten, der Kompromiss läge darin
Dictating a precise written agreement both accept
scoringCriteria: each party addressed in a fitting register
final agreement precise and accepted by both
priorityErrors: one register used for both parties

help.intro: A eulogy for a ficus, written completely straight. If it makes the reader smile, the smile must come from the situation — the moment your language winks, you have fallen off the rope.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Play it straight or not at all
tips.text: The comedy is structural: solemn form, absurd subject. Add a joke and you have neither comedy nor register control. Write as if Herbert's family were in the second row.

tips.title: Dignity, plant-sized
tips.text: "Er verlangte wenig: Licht, ein wenig Wasser, dann und wann ein gutes Wort. Nicht einmal das Wenige haben wir ihm zuverlässig gegeben." True, measured, and it holds.

speaking.topic: The hardest brief in the course: a eulogy for a deceased houseplant, in genuine, dignified eulogy register — graded on the tone tightrope, never on jokes.
practisePoints: Holding a dignified register over an absurd subject
Eulogy conventions: address, virtue, memory, farewell
Elevated lexis that stays warm, not stiff
speaking.material:
Writing task:
- Write a eulogy (120–150 words) for Ficus "Herbert", who stood eight years by the office window and has died of neglect during the summer holidays.
- The register is REAL eulogy German: elevated, warm, measured — Trauerrede, not sketch comedy. The absurdity lives entirely in the subject; the language never winks.
Rubric (grade against this):
- Tone tightrope (biggest weight): every sentence must be sayable at a real funeral. One joke word or ironic aside = points off; unearned pathos ("Held", "Tragödie") likewise.
- Eulogy conventions present: address to the mourners, a remembered virtue, a shared memory, a farewell formula.
- Elevated but living register: Konjunktiv and formal lexis without museum stiffness.
- Structure: opening address → life → what he gave us → farewell.

help.intro: One story, five voices, no time to think. The AI calls "Märchen!" and your very next sentence must sound centuries old — while Frau Berger and her key march on unbroken.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Lead with the marker
tips.text: Open the shifted sentence with the genre's loudest signal: "Es war einmal …" for Märchen, "Wie soeben bekannt wurde …" for Nachrichten, "Hiermit wird …" for Amtsdeutsch. The first four words buy the whole register.

tips.title: Continuity is half the score
tips.text: A dazzling Werbespot sentence that forgets the key earns half. Before speaking, grab one noun from the previous sentence and carry it across the genre border with you.

speaking.topic: An improvised chain story: we alternate sentences, and you inject genre shifts by announcing the new genre before your sentence. My next sentence must land the new register instantly while keeping the story coherent.
practisePoints: Instant register hits on an announced genre
Keeping story continuity through every shift
Genre markers: Präteritum menace, Märchen inversion, Amtsdeutsch nominal style
scoringCriteria: continuity of key, character and detail
speed — no stalling before a shifted sentence
speaking.material:
Story skeleton and rules:
- Seed: "Als Frau Berger am Montag ihren Briefkasten öffnete, lag darin ein einzelner, sehr alter Schlüssel." You start.
- We alternate single sentences. Every 2–3 turns you call a genre shift BEFORE your sentence: Krimi → Märchen → Nachrichtensprecher → Werbespot → Behördenschreiben (use at least four of these, any order).
- Required register markers I must hit: Krimi = terse präteritum and menace; Märchen = "Es war einmal"-tone, inversion, archaic flavour; Nachrichten = neutral report, passive, attribution; Werbespot = imperatives, superlatives, direct address; Behördenschreiben = nominal style, "hiermit", "fristgerecht".
- Continuity rule: the key, Frau Berger and one detail from the previous sentence must survive every shift.
- Score each of my sentences for register accuracy AND story continuity; a perfect register that breaks the story earns half.

help.intro: Not the gate — the dress rehearsal. Easy questions are the trap: "Was machst du am Wochenende?" now demands an essayist's answer. Prove the whole staircase lives in one voice.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Simple question, layered answer
tips.text: Answer the fact, then the meaning: "Am Wochenende koche ich — wobei Kochen für mich weniger Ernährung ist als die einzige Stunde, in der niemand etwas von mir will." Fact, then essay.

tips.title: Ease shrinks range
tips.text: On comfortable topics your grammar quietly retreats to A2. Plant one Konjunktiv, one passive and one FVG per answer on purpose until the range comes uninvited.

speaking.topic: The capstone rehearsal: a ten-question full-range interview in which A1 topics demand C2 answers. Ask beginner questions — family, hobbies, my town, food, weekend — and require essayist depth: nuance, structure, imagery, register control ("Erzählen Sie von Ihrer Familie — als Essayist").
practisePoints: Elevating trivial topics to essayistic depth
Full grammar range recycled: Konjunktiv, passive, FVG
Structure and imagery inside spoken answers

help.intro: The last door of the course: one dinner party, three impossible guests, twelve exchanges. Everything you have built — registers, repair, mediation, particles — sits at this table. Host it.

tips.title: How this course works
tips.text: Copy the exercise into your AI assistant (voice mode is best), do the exercise there, and paste the score it gives you back here. Stay with one assistant so your scores stay comparable.

tips.title: Be the table's conductor
tips.text: Relay between guests instead of answering each alone: "Herr Doktor, was sagen SIE denn zu dieser These?" — handing the provocateur to the pedant is peak discourse management, and it buys you a breath.

tips.title: Three guests, three registers
tips.text: Pedant: full formal, concede precision gladly. Provocateur: cool, one concession then a counter. Mumbler: relaxed du-register — and if you missed it, "Wie meinst du das genau?" is a host's right.

speaking.topic: The finale: "Der Salon". I host a dinner party; you play THREE guests in distinct voices: a pedant who corrects everything (formal, precise), a provocateur who drops outrageous theses (sharp, baiting), and a mumbler who speaks in fast colloquial contractions (isses, haste, 'nen). Rotate them, let them talk over each other, and make me host all three for the full twelve exchanges: soothe the pedant, parry the provocateur, decode the mumbler, and keep one conversation alive between them.
practisePoints: Register agility across three simultaneous voices
Discourse management: turn-taking, soothing, redirecting
Decoding colloquial speech live and relaying it upward
Grace under provocation — parry without escalation
scoringCriteria: each guest answered in a fitting register
the table held together as one conversation
